 {
   "description": "Hey Reachy is a native client for the Reachy Mini desktop robots — one app for iPhone, iPad and Mac.

TRY IT WITHOUT A ROBOT

The Connect screen's third segment starts a session against a simulator the app carries itself. It needs no robot, no network and no account: the robot's own description is drawn and moved by the same kinematics the app sends to real hardware. The joystick moves it and the 3D model follows. The simulator has no camera, no app catalogue and no Wi-Fi setup, because those belong to a machine that does not exist.

A Reachy Mini Wireless on your network is what the whole app is for. A Lite model — or a daemon run in simulation on a computer — connects the same way, minus the routes only the wireless daemon serves.

WHAT IT DOES

• Connect — three ways in: Local (a network sweep, Bonjour, an address you type, and on a Mac the daemon on this very computer), HF (your robots from outside their network, through the Hugging Face relay), and Simulator. Robots are identified by hardware id, so the same robot at a new address is still the same robot.

• Live control — joystick teleop of the 6-DoF head, the antennas and body rotation, with the robot's camera and two-way audio, so you can talk through its speaker. Let the head follow a face, at a strength you pick between a glance and a lock.

• 3D viewer — a RealityKit model built from the robot's own URDF and meshes, mirroring it in real time.

• Moves — browse and play the recorded moves the robot ships with, from the app or by asking Siri for one by name. Record your own takes straight from the phone: drive the robot with the joystick, then play the take back.

• Sounds — a soundboard for the robot's speaker. Add audio files on your device, send them across and play them with a tap. The library is kept on the device, so a robot that restarts and loses its copy is given it again on the next play.

• Apps — install, update and remove robot apps from Hugging Face Spaces, following each job as it runs. Filter and sort the catalogue and pin the apps you use most. The robot wakes itself before an app starts and parks again when it lets go.

• State — the control loop's frequency, worst interval and error count charted live, beside the robot's own processor, memory, temperature and uptime.

• Files — an SFTP browser for the robot's filesystem.

• Bluetooth setup and recovery — put a brand-new robot onto Wi-Fi over an encrypted Bluetooth channel, or bring back one that fell off the network.

AT HOME ON YOUR DEVICES

Widgets for the Home Screen, the Lock Screen, StandBy and the Mac's Notification Centre. The Mac also keeps the robot in the menu bar: awake or asleep, one button to change it, and the installed apps underneath. Control Center controls for power, for a move or an app you choose yourself, for a sound, and for stopping whatever is running — each one on the Lock Screen and the Action button too. Siri and Shortcuts for waking, sleeping, powering off, launching an app, playing a move, or asking whether the robot is awake and what is running on it — and each of those can name which robot it means, so two Reachys on one desk are told apart. Six accent themes, each with a matching app icon. English, German, Spanish, French and Russian.

PRIVACY

Nothing is collected. The app talks to your robot on your own network and, if you choose to sign in, to Hugging Face with your own account. There is no server on our side.

A NOTE ON YOUR NETWORK

The robot's daemon provides no authentication and no encryption of its own. Use Hey Reachy on a trusted private network or on the robot's own access point — never through a port forward or a public address.

Hey Reachy is unofficial and is not affiliated with, endorsed by or supported by Pollen Robotics. It is an independent client for the robot daemon's documented HTTP and WebSocket API. "Reachy Mini" is a product name of Pollen Robotics, used here solely to describe what this app is compatible with.

Requires iOS 18 or macOS 15.",

A Reachy Mini Lite, and a daemon run in simulation on a computer, connect like a Wireless one. The app reads which kind it reached and offers only what that kind serves — and it no longer hides the camera of a robot that has one. On a Mac, the daemon running on this very computer gets a row of its own.

The robot sits in the menu bar: awake or asleep, one button to change it, and the installed apps underneath. The widgets reach the Mac too.

Three segments instead of four. The address field now sits under the list of found robots, which is where the reader goes the moment that list stays empty.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud (requires claude.ai account access)); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	import ProjectDescription
2	
3	/// The app and its widget extension are separate processes with separate
4	/// containers, so anything both must read — the known robots, the snapshot the
5	/// widget renders — lives in this group rather than in either container.
6	let appGroup = "group.com.alexey1312.ReachyMini"
7	
8	let project = Project(
9	    name: "ReachyMiniApps",
10	    packages: [
11	        // Local ReachyKit SPM package at the repo root
12	        .package(path: ".."),
13	        // Prefire renders SwiftUI previews as snapshots and as a browsable playbook. It is
14	        // declared here rather than in Package.swift because its generated tests and its
15	        // PlaybookView both call UIKit unconditionally — the root package still builds for macOS.
16	        // Exact, not `upToNextMajor`: `ReachyUISnapshotTests/PreviewTests.stencil` is a fork of
17	        // this version's built-in test template, and a floated minor would render it against a
18	        // changed set of Stencil arguments.
19	        .remote(url: "https://github.com/BarredEwe/Prefire", requirement: .exact("5.7.0")),
20	        .remote(
21	            url: "https://github.com/pointfreeco/swift-snapshot-testing",
22	            requirement: .upToNextMajor(from: "1.19.4")
23	        ),
24	    ],
25	    settings: .settings(
26	        // One version for the app and the widget: App Store validation requires
27	        // the extension's CFBundleShortVersionString to match its host's.
28	        base: [
29	            // Beta: the first tag is 0.1.0, and the tag and the shipped version
30	            // have to be the same number to be worth reading.
31	            "MARKETING_VERSION": "0.4.1",
32	            "CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION": "1",
33	        ],
34	        configurations: [
35	            // Set project-wide rather than per target: the previews and the playbook reach ReachyUI's
36	            // internal screens through `@testable import`, and it is the *package* target that has to
37	            // be built with testability for that to link.
38	            .debug(name: .debug, settings: ["ENABLE_TESTABILITY": "YES"]),
39	            .release(name: .release),
40	        ]
41	    ),
42	    targets: [
43	        .target(
44	            name: "ReachyMini",
45	            destinations: [.iPhone, .iPad, .mac],
46	            product: .app,
47	            bundleId: "com.alexey1312.ReachyMini",
48	            deploymentTargets: .multiplatform(iOS: "18.0", macOS: "15.0"),
49	            infoPlist: .extendingDefault(with: [
50	                // The product name is the internal identifier; this is the brand.
51	                "CFBundleDisplayName": .string("Hey Reachy"),
52	                "CFBundleName": .string("Hey Reachy"),
53	                // What `\(.applicationName)` in `ReachyShortcuts` resolves to, and
54	                // the display name alone reads badly inside a phrase: "Wake up Hey
55	                // Reachy". Siri matches every phrase against these as well.
56	                // Deliberately not "Reachy Mini" — that is the name of Pollen's own
57	                // app, and on a phone carrying both it would be ambiguous.
58	                // **Siri only, and it is not a Spotlight key** — QA1950 describes it
59	                // as the spoken form and says nothing about typed search, so adding
60	                // a word here does nothing for a query in the search field. That
61	                // half is `Navigation/SpotlightIndex.swift`. Apple's own note there:
62	                // put synonyms in it, never the display name itself.
63	                "INAlternativeAppNames": .array([
64	                    .dictionary(["INAlternativeAppName": .string("Reachy")]),
65	                ]),
66	                "CFBundleShortVersionString": .string("$(MARKETING_VERSION)"),
67	                "CFBundleVersion": .string("$(CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION)"),
68	                // Spelled out because `actool` does not write it: it fills
69	                // CFBundleIcons from the catalogue and leaves the top level
70	                // empty, which App Store Connect rejects the upload over. Found
71	                // by unpacking the exported .ipa, not by any build warning.
72	                "CFBundleIconName": .string("AppIcon"),
73	                // ITMS-90683: WebRTC (and RealityKit via ARKit) reference the
74	                // capture APIs, so the string is required even though the app
75	                // never records with the phone's camera. Say exactly that.
76	                "NSCameraUsageDescription": .string(
77	                    "Hey Reachy never records with your phone's camera; the robot video stack references this API."
78	                ),
79	                // HTTPS-exempt encryption only; answered here once so App Store
80	                // Connect never asks per build.
81	                "ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption": .boolean(false),
82	                "LSApplicationCategoryType": .string("public.app-category.utilities"),
83	                // Phase 0.4 device checks: Local Network permission + Bonjour + ATS
84	                "NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription": .string(
85	                    "Discovers and connects to your Reachy Mini robot on the local network."
86	                ),
87	                "NSBonjourServices": .array([
88	                    .string("_reachy-mini._tcp"),
89	                    .string("_http._tcp"),
90	                ]),
91	                "NSAppTransportSecurity": .dictionary([
92	                    "NSAllowsLocalNetworking": .boolean(true),
93	                ]),
94	                // BLE Wi-Fi provisioning. The only key a foreground central needs on
95	                // iOS 18: no capability, and no pairing prompt either, since the robot
96	                // registers a NoInputNoOutput Just-Works agent.
97	                // NSBluetoothPeripheralUsageDescription is iOS 12 and earlier — omitted.
98	                "NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription": .string(
99	                    "Sets up your Reachy Mini's Wi-Fi and recovers a robot that can't reach the network."
100	                ),
101	                // Phase 2 camera: WebRTC mic uplink (client mic → robot speaker)
102	                "NSMicrophoneUsageDescription": .string(
103	                    "Talk to people near your Reachy Mini through its speaker."
104	                ),
105	                "UILaunchScreen": .dictionary([:]),
106	                // The UIScene lifecycle is a launch requirement under the iOS 27
107	                // SDK, and SwiftUI's `App` being scene-based is not the same as
108	                // this app *declaring* it — Tuist's `.extendingDefault` does not
109	                // supply the manifest, so nothing here said so.
110	                //
111	                // **No `UISceneConfigurations`, deliberately.** The one scene is
112	                // configured in code: `QuickActionAppDelegate` answers
113	                // `configurationForConnecting` with a `UISceneConfiguration(name:
114	                // nil, …)` naming `QuickActionSceneDelegate`, which is the only way
115	                // to be told a Home Screen quick action was tapped. Listing a
116	                // configuration here would give UIKit a second, disagreeing answer
117	                // about the delegate class; declaring adoption and leaving the
118	                // configuration to the delegate is the combination Apple documents
119	                // for an app that builds its own.
120	                "UIApplicationSceneManifest": .dictionary([
121	                    "UIApplicationSupportsMultipleScenes": .boolean(false),
122	                ]),
123	                // Read by `KnownRobots`, which is in a library and so cannot know
124	                // one developer account's group. The extension declares the same.
125	                "ReachyAppGroupIdentifier": .string(appGroup),
126	                // The widget opens the app through this scheme. It is the one the
127	                // OAuth callback already uses: an app gets a scheme, and
128	                // `ASWebAuthenticationSession` claims the callback while a sign-in
129	                // is running regardless of what is registered here.
130	                "CFBundleURLTypes": .array([
131	                    .dictionary([
132	                        "CFBundleURLName": .string("com.alexey1312.ReachyMini"),
133	                        "CFBundleURLSchemes": .array([.string("reachy-mini-swift")]),
134	                    ]),
135	                ]),
136	                // The literal value of `CSSearchableItemActionType`, which is how a
137	                // tapped Spotlight row reaches `RootLifecycle`. Sources disagree
138	                // about whether a *system* activity type has to be declared here at
139	                // all — a custom one certainly does — and the failure mode if it
140	                // does is silent: the rows are found, the tap opens the app, and it
141	                // lands on whatever tab was last selected. Declaring it costs one
142	                // line and settles the question. `Navigation/SpotlightIndex.swift`.
143	                "NSUserActivityTypes": .array([
144	                    .string("com.apple.corespotlightitem"),
145	                ]),
146	            ]),
147	            sources: ["ReachyMini/Sources/**"],
148	            // The five themed icons are iOS-only inputs. macOS has no alternate
149	            // icons at all, so its `actool` compiles them and then drops them —
150	            // measured: the macOS `Assets.car` carries `AppIcon` and nothing else.
151	            // Scoping them saves that work. It is **not** what fixed the macOS asset
152	            // compilation on CI — that needed a newer Xcode, and `ci.yml` says which.
153	            resources: [
154	                .glob(
155	                    pattern: "ReachyMini/Resources/**",
156	                    excluding: ["ReachyMini/Resources/AppIcon-*.icon"]
157	                ),
158	                .glob(
159	                    pattern: "ReachyMini/Resources/AppIcon-*.icon",
160	                    inclusionCondition: .when([.ios])
161	                ),
162	            ],
163	            dependencies: [
164	                .package(product: "ReachyKit"),
165	                .package(product: "ReachyUI"),
166	                // The intents live there so the widget extension can reach the same
167	                // ones; the shortcuts provider that exposes them to Siri has to be
168	                // in this bundle.
169	                .package(product: "ReachyWidgetUI"),
170	                // No longer conditional: the extension has a Mac destination, so the
171	                // macOS app embeds it and the Mac gets the two reading widgets.
172	                .target(name: "ReachyWidget"),
173	            ],
174	            // Two files rather than one generated dictionary: the macOS build is
175	            // sandboxed and hardened for Developer ID, and those keys are
176	            // macOS-only — signing an iOS build with them fails against any
177	            // provisioning profile. The `[sdk=macosx*]` override picks per SDK.
178	            settings: .settings(base: [
179	                "SWIFT_VERSION": "6.0",
180	                "CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS": "ReachyMini/Entitlements/ReachyMini-iOS.entitlements",
181	                "CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS[sdk=macosx*]": "ReachyMini/Entitlements/ReachyMini-macOS.entitlements",
182	                // Notarization rejects a Developer ID app without it: the executable
183	                // signs with flags=0x0 and the notary answers "does not have the
184	                // hardened runtime enabled" per architecture.
185	                "ENABLE_HARDENED_RUNTIME[sdk=macosx*]": "YES",
186	                // SDK-scoped because macOS has no alternate icons: an unscoped
187	                // setting names five bundles the macOS build has no use for.
188	                // Every name here must equal a `ReachyTheme.alternateIconName`
189	                // and a committed `.icon` directory — `ThemeIconNameTests` reads
190	                // this literal back and fails when the three drift.
191	                "ASSETCATALOG_COMPILER_ALTERNATE_APPICON_NAMES[sdk=iphone*]":
192	                    "AppIcon-Bronze AppIcon-Teal AppIcon-Indigo AppIcon-Orchid AppIcon-Rose",
193	                "ASSETCATALOG_COMPILER_INCLUDE_ALL_APPICON_ASSETS[sdk=iphone*]": "YES",
194	            ])
195	        ),
196	        // Deliberately thin: a timeline provider over the shared snapshot and a
197	        // view. It depends on ReachyWidgetUI rather than ReachyUI so that a
198	        // process woken for a moment does not link WebRTC and RealityKit.
199	        .target(
200	            name: "ReachyWidget",
201	            destinations: [.iPhone, .iPad, .mac],
202	            product: .appExtension,
203	            bundleId: "com.alexey1312.ReachyMini.Widget",
204	            deploymentTargets: .multiplatform(iOS: "18.0", macOS: "15.0"),
205	            infoPlist: .extendingDefault(with: [
206	                "CFBundleDisplayName": .string("Hey Reachy"),
207	                "CFBundleShortVersionString": .string("$(MARKETING_VERSION)"),
208	                "CFBundleVersion": .string("$(CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION)"),
209	                "ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption": .boolean(false),
210	                // Its own process, so it needs its own copy of the group name.
211	                "ReachyAppGroupIdentifier": .string(appGroup),
212	                // The control buttons run their intent in *this* process, and it
213	                // talks to the robot over plain HTTP on the LAN. Without the ATS
214	                // exception that request is refused before it leaves the device;
215	                // the usage string is what the system would show if it ever had a
216	                // screen to ask from, which an extension does not — so the
217	                // permission has to already exist from the app having connected.
218	                "NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription": .string(
219	                    "Wakes your Reachy Mini and starts its apps on the local network."
220	                ),
221	                "NSBonjourServices": .array([
222	                    .string("_reachy-mini._tcp"),
223	                    .string("_http._tcp"),
224	                ]),
225	                "NSAppTransportSecurity": .dictionary([
226	                    "NSAllowsLocalNetworking": .boolean(true),
227	                ]),
228	                "NSExtension": .dictionary([
229	                    "NSExtensionPointIdentifier": .string("com.apple.widgetkit-extension"),
230	                ]),
231	            ]),
232	            sources: ["ReachyWidget/Sources/**"],
233	            dependencies: [
234	                .package(product: "ReachyKit"),
235	                .package(product: "ReachyWidgetUI"),
236	                // Declared even though `ReachyWidgetUI` already links it: Swift needs a
237	                // direct dependency to `import` a module, and this target's controls name
238	                // their titles with `.reachy(_:)`.
239	                .package(product: "ReachyDesign"),
240	            ],
241	            // Two files rather than the one generated dictionary this used to carry,
242	            // for the reason the app target states: a macOS app extension must be
243	            // sandboxed, and `com.apple.security.app-sandbox` is a macOS-only key
244	            // that fails an iOS build against any provisioning profile.
245	            settings: .settings(base: [
246	                "SWIFT_VERSION": "6.0",
247	                "CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS": "ReachyWidget/Entitlements/ReachyWidget-iOS.entitlements",
248	                "CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS[sdk=macosx*]":
249	                    "ReachyWidget/Entitlements/ReachyWidget-macOS.entitlements",
250	                // The notary reads every executable in the bundle, not only the app's,
251	                // so an extension needs this as much as its host — see the app target.
252	                "ENABLE_HARDENED_RUNTIME[sdk=macosx*]": "YES",
253	            ])
254	        ),
255	        // Smoke tests: the one thing snapshots cannot see is the app binary itself
256	        // booting. iOS-only — XCUITest on macOS needs Accessibility permission on
257	        // the runner, which CI cannot grant.
258	        .target(
259	            name: "ReachyMiniUITests",
260	            destinations: [.iPhone, .iPad],
261	            product: .uiTests,
262	            bundleId: "com.alexey1312.ReachyMiniUITests",
263	            deploymentTargets: .iOS("18.0"),
264	            infoPlist: .default,
265	            sources: ["ReachyMiniUITests/Sources/**"],
266	            dependencies: [
267	                .target(name: "ReachyMini"),
268	            ]
269	        ),
270	        .target(
271	            name: "ReachyStorybook",
272	            destinations: [.iPhone, .iPad],
273	            product: .app,
274	            bundleId: "com.alexey1312.ReachyMiniStorybook",
275	            deploymentTargets: .multiplatform(iOS: "18.0"),
276	            infoPlist: .extendingDefault(with: [
277	                // No Bonjour or ATS keys: the storybook renders fixtures and never reaches the network.
278	                "UILaunchScreen": .dictionary([:]),
279	            ]),
280	            // `PrefirePlaybookPlugin` is deliberately absent: it only ever scans the sources of
281	            // the target it is attached to (`GeneratePlaybookCommand` ignores the config's
282	            // `sources`, and `playbook_configuration` has no such key), so it cannot see the
283	            // previews that live in ReachyUI. `mise run storybook` runs the CLI instead.
284	            // `DeviceCheckView` belongs to ReachyMini, which an app target cannot import; its two
285	            // source files are compiled in directly so the catalogue can show that screen too.
286	            sources: [
287	                "ReachyStorybook/Sources/**",
288	                "ReachyStorybook/Generated/**",
289	                "../Sources/ReachyDesign/Previews/**",
290	                "../Sources/ReachyUI/Previews/**",
291	                "../Sources/ReachyWidgetUI/Previews/**",
292	                "ReachyMini/Sources/DeviceCheckView.swift",
293	                "ReachyMini/Sources/DeviceCheckModel.swift",
294	                "ReachyMini/Previews/**",
295	            ],
296	            dependencies: [
297	                .package(product: "ReachyDesign"),
298	                .package(product: "ReachyUI"),
299	                .package(product: "ReachyWidgetUI"),
300	                .package(product: "Prefire"),
301	            ]
302	        ),
303	        .target(
304	            name: "ReachyUISnapshotTests",
305	            destinations: [.iPhone, .iPad],
306	            product: .unitTests,
307	            bundleId: "com.alexey1312.ReachyUISnapshotTests",
308	            deploymentTargets: .multiplatform(iOS: "18.0"),
309	            sources: [
310	                "ReachyUISnapshotTests/Sources/**",
311	                "../Sources/ReachyDesign/Previews/**",
312	                "../Sources/ReachyUI/Previews/**",
313	                "../Sources/ReachyWidgetUI/Previews/**",
314	                "ReachyMini/Sources/DeviceCheckView.swift",
315	                "ReachyMini/Sources/DeviceCheckModel.swift",
316	                "ReachyMini/Previews/**",
317	            ],

2	  "description": "Hey Reachy is a native client for the Reachy Mini desktop robots — one app for iPhone, iPad and Mac.

TRY IT WITHOUT A ROBOT

The Connect screen's third segment starts a session against a simulator the app carries itself. It needs no robot, no network and no account: the robot's own description is drawn and moved by the same kinematics the app sends to real hardware. The joystick moves it and the 3D model follows. The simulator has no camera, no app catalogue and no Wi-Fi setup, because those belong to a machine that does not exist.

A Reachy Mini Wireless on your network is what the whole app is for. A Lite model — or a daemon run in simulation on a computer — connects the same way, minus the routes only the wireless daemon serves.

WHAT IT DOES

• Connect — three ways in: Local (a network sweep, Bonjour, an address you type, and on a Mac the daemon on this very computer), HF (your robots from outside their network, through the Hugging Face relay), and Simulator. Robots are identified by hardware id, so the same robot at a new address is still the same robot.

• Live control — joystick teleop of the 6-DoF head, the antennas and body rotation, with the robot's camera and two-way audio, so you can talk through its speaker. Let the head follow a face, at a strength you pick between a glance and a lock.

• 3D viewer — a RealityKit model built from the robot's own URDF and meshes, mirroring it in real time.

• Moves — browse and play the recorded moves the robot ships with, from the app or by asking Siri for one by name. Record your own takes straight from the phone: drive the robot with the joystick, then play the take back.

• Sounds — a soundboard for the robot's speaker. Add audio files on your device, send them across and play them with a tap. The library is kept on the device, so a robot that restarts and loses its copy is given it again on the next play.

• Apps — install, update and remove robot apps from Hugging Face Spaces, following each job as it runs. Filter and sort the catalogue and pin the apps you use most. The robot wakes itself before an app starts and parks again when it lets go.

• State — the control loop's frequency, worst interval and error count charted live, beside the robot's own processor, memory, temperature and uptime.

• Files — an SFTP browser for the robot's filesystem.

• Bluetooth setup and recovery — put a brand-new robot onto Wi-Fi over an encrypted Bluetooth channel, or bring back one that fell off the network.

AT HOME ON YOUR DEVICES

Widgets for the Home Screen, the Lock Screen, StandBy and the Mac's Notification Centre. The Mac also keeps the robot in the menu bar: awake or asleep, one button to change it, and the installed apps underneath. Control Center controls for power, for a move or an app you choose yourself, for a sound, and for stopping whatever is running — each one on the Lock Screen and the Action button too. Siri and Shortcuts for waking, sleeping, powering off, launching an app, playing a move, or asking whether the robot is awake and what is running on it — and each of those can name which robot it means, so two Reachys on one desk are told apart. Six accent themes, each with a matching app icon. English, German, Spanish, French and Russian.

PRIVACY

Nothing is collected. The app talks to your robot on your own network and, if you choose to sign in, to Hugging Face with your own account. There is no server on our side.

A NOTE ON YOUR NETWORK

The robot's daemon provides no authentication and no encryption of its own. Use Hey Reachy on a trusted private network or on the robot's own access point — never through a port forward or a public address.

Hey Reachy is unofficial and is not affiliated with, endorsed by or supported by Pollen Robotics. It is an independent client for the robot daemon's documented HTTP and WebSocket API. "Reachy Mini" is a product name of Pollen Robotics, used here solely to describe what this app is compatible with.

content.text:
Both changed files are purely release-metadata:

1. **`Apps/Project.swift`** — a one-line `MARKETING_VERSION` string bump from `"0.4.0"` to `"0.4.1"`. No sources, sinks, entitlements, permissions, entry points, or logic changed. The bundle id, entitlements, sandbox/hardened-runtime settings, ATS exceptions, Bonjour service list, URL scheme, app-group id, and usage strings are all untouched.

2. **`metadata/version/0.4.1/en-US.json`** — one added sentence in the `whatsNew` copy. This is App Store Connect release-notes text; it is never executed, never rendered inside the app, and never reaches any sink. `description`, `keywords`, `promotionalText`, `supportUrl`, `marketingUrl` are unchanged.

No new entry points, no new sinks, no data flow to trace, no gate/allowlist/registry/permission edits. Nothing in either file is attacker-influenceable, and neither file participates in runtime code paths.
